data.scenario_text: The function L(x)=8\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(x-4)\right]+30 models the water level, in feet, of a reservoir, where x=1 represents January, x=2 represents February, and so on.
data.part_a: What is the average water level of the reservoir?
data.part_b: What are the highest and lowest water levels of the reservoir?
data.part_c: What is the period of this function, and what does it mean in this context?
data.part_d: What is the phase shift of this function, and what does it mean in this context?
data.part_e: Use the model to estimate the water level in November. Round to the nearest tenth of a foot.
data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline y=D is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=30, so the reservoir averages \boxed{30\text{ ft}}.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=8, so the quantity rises 8 above the average value and falls 8 below it:

\text{maximum}=30+8=38\text{ ft}\qquad\text{minimum}=30-8=22\text{ ft}

The reservoir is highest in July at 38\text{ ft} and lowest in January at 22\text{ ft}, so the range of levels is \boxed{[22\text{ ft},\ 38\text{ ft}]}.

Part (c). Here B=\frac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\pi/6}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} months, and so the level follows a yearly cycle and repeats every 12 months.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of x that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-4)=0 \implies x-4=0 \implies x=4

The phase shift is \boxed{4} months, and so the pattern is shifted 4 months to the right: the level is at its average and rising in April, peaks in July, and is lowest in January.

Part (e). Substitute x=11 (November):

L(11)=8\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(11-4)\right]+30=8\sin\left(\frac{7\pi}{6}\right)+30

=8\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)+30=26

So the model gives exactly \boxed{26.0\text{ ft}} in November.

data.scenario_text: The function d(x)=4\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(x-5)\right]+14 models the depth of the water, in feet, at a harbor, where x=0 represents midnight and x is the number of hours after midnight.
data.part_a: What is the average depth of the water at this harbor?
data.part_b: What are the greatest and least depths of the water at this harbor?
data.part_c: What is the period of this function? How many times does high tide occur in a day?
data.part_d: What is the phase shift of this function, and what does it mean in this context?
data.part_e: Use the model to estimate the depth of the water at 7:00 a.m.. Round to the nearest tenth of a foot.
data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline of a sinusoid d(x)=A\sin[B(x-h)]+D is y=D, and the midline is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=14, so the water averages \boxed{14\text{ ft}} deep.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=4, so the quantity rises 4 above the average value and falls 4 below it:

\text{maximum}=14+4=18\text{ ft}\qquad\text{minimum}=14-4=10\text{ ft}

High tide is at 8:00 a.m., when the depth is 18\text{ ft}, and low tide is at 2:00 p.m., when the depth is 10\text{ ft}, so the range of depths is \boxed{[10\text{ ft},\ 18\text{ ft}]}.

Part (c). Here B=\frac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\pi/6}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} hours, and so the water returns to the same depth every 12 hours. High tide therefore occurs twice in a 24-hour day, and low tide twice as well.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of x that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-5)=0 \implies x-5=0 \implies x=5

The phase shift is \boxed{5} hours, and so the pattern is shifted 5 hours to the right: at 5:00 a.m. the water is at its average depth and rising. High tide is at 8:00 a.m. and again at 8:00 p.m.; low tide is at 2:00 p.m. and again at 2:00 a.m..

Part (e). Substitute x=7 (7:00 a.m.):

d(7)=4\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(7-5)\right]+14=4\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{3}\right)+14

=4\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)+14=\frac{4\sqrt{3}}{2}+14

So the model gives approximately \boxed{17.5\text{ ft}} at 7:00 a.m..

data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline of a sinusoid d(x)=A\sin[B(x-h)]+D is y=D, and the midline is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=12, so the water averages \boxed{12\text{ ft}} deep.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=4, so the quantity rises 4 above the average value and falls 4 below it:

\text{maximum}=12+4=16\text{ ft}\qquad\text{minimum}=12-4=8\text{ ft}

High tide is at 8:00 a.m., when the depth is 16\text{ ft}, and low tide is at 2:00 p.m., when the depth is 8\text{ ft}, so the range of depths is \boxed{[8\text{ ft},\ 16\text{ ft}]}.

Part (c). Here B=\frac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\pi/6}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} hours, and so the water returns to the same depth every 12 hours. High tide therefore occurs twice in a 24-hour day, and low tide twice as well.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of x that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-5)=0 \implies x-5=0 \implies x=5

The phase shift is \boxed{5} hours, and so the pattern is shifted 5 hours to the right: at 5:00 a.m. the water is at its average depth and rising. High tide is at 8:00 a.m. and again at 8:00 p.m.; low tide is at 2:00 p.m. and again at 2:00 a.m..

Part (e). Substitute x=9 (9:00 a.m.):

d(9)=4\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(9-5)\right]+12=4\sin\left(\frac{2\pi}{3}\right)+12

=4\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)+12=\frac{4\sqrt{3}}{2}+12

\text{maximum}=31+20=51\text{ ft}\qquad\text{minimum}=31-20=11\text{ ft}

Part (c). Here B=\frac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\pi/6}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of t that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

data.part_e: Use the model to estimate the household's electricity use in May. Round to the nearest kilowatt-hour.
data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline y=D is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=828, so the household averages \boxed{828\text{ kWh}} per month.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=122, so the quantity rises 122 above the average value and falls 122 below it:

\text{maximum}=828+122=950\text{ kWh}\qquad\text{minimum}=828-122=706\text{ kWh}

The heaviest use is in July at 950\text{ kWh} and the lightest is in January at 706\text{ kWh}, so the range of monthly use is \boxed{[706\text{ kWh},\ 950\text{ kWh}]}.

Part (c). Here B=\frac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\pi/6}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} months, and so use follows a yearly cycle and repeats every 12 months.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of x that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-4)=0 \implies x-4=0 \implies x=4

The phase shift is \boxed{4} months, and so the pattern is shifted 4 months to the right: use is at its average and rising in April, peaks in July, and bottoms out in January.

Part (e). Substitute x=5 (May):

E(5)=122\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(5-4)\right]+828=122\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{6}\right)+828

=122\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)+828=889

data.part_b: What are the rider's greatest and least heights above the ground?

data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline y=D is the average value of the oscillation, and for a rider on a wheel that is the height of the wheel's center, because the rider spends equal time above and below it. Here D=40, so the rider averages \boxed{40\text{ ft}} above the ground.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=22, so the quantity rises 22 above the average value and falls 22 below it:

\text{maximum}=40+22=62\text{ ft}\qquad\text{minimum}=40-22=18\text{ ft}

The rider reaches a maximum of 62\text{ ft} at 5 minutes after the ride starts and a minimum of 18\text{ ft} at 11 minutes after the ride starts, so the range of heights is \boxed{[18\text{ ft},\ 62\text{ ft}]}. That minimum is also the height of the boarding platform.

Part (c). Here B=\frac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\pi/6}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} minutes, and so the wheel makes one full revolution every 12 minutes.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of t that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(t-2)=0 \implies t-2=0 \implies t=2

The phase shift is \boxed{2} minutes, and so the ride is shifted 2 minutes: the rider is at the height of the center and rising at 2 minutes after the ride starts, reaches the top at 5 minutes after the ride starts, and is lowest at 11 minutes after the ride starts.

Part (e). Substitute t=7 (at 7 minutes after the ride starts):

H(7)=22\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(7-2)\right]+40=22\sin\left(\frac{5\pi}{6}\right)+40

=22\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)+40=51

So the model gives exactly \boxed{51.0\text{ ft}} at 7 minutes after the ride starts.

data.part_b: What are the greatest and least depths of the water at this harbor?
data.part_c: What is the period of this function? How many times does high tide occur in a day?
data.part_d: What is the phase shift of this function, and what does it mean in this context?
data.part_e: Use the model to estimate the depth of the water at noon. Round to the nearest tenth of a foot.
data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline of a sinusoid d(x)=A\sin[B(x-h)]+D is y=D, and the midline is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=14, so the water averages \boxed{14\text{ ft}} deep.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=4, so the quantity rises 4 above the average value and falls 4 below it:

\text{maximum}=14+4=18\text{ ft}\qquad\text{minimum}=14-4=10\text{ ft}

High tide is at 5:00 a.m., when the depth is 18\text{ ft}, and low tide is at 11:00 a.m., when the depth is 10\text{ ft}, so the range of depths is \boxed{[10\text{ ft},\ 18\text{ ft}]}.

Part (c). Here B=\frac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\pi/6}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} hours, and so the water returns to the same depth every 12 hours. High tide therefore occurs twice in a 24-hour day, and low tide twice as well.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of x that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-2)=0 \implies x-2=0 \implies x=2

The phase shift is \boxed{2} hours, and so the pattern is shifted 2 hours to the right: at 2:00 a.m. the water is at its average depth and rising. High tide is at 5:00 a.m. and again at 5:00 p.m.; low tide is at 11:00 a.m. and again at 11:00 p.m..

Part (e). Substitute x=12 (noon):

d(12)=4\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(12-2)\right]+14=4\sin\left(\frac{5\pi}{3}\right)+14

=4\left(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)+14=-\frac{4\sqrt{3}}{2}+14

So the model gives approximately \boxed{10.5\text{ ft}} at noon.

Part (a). The midline y=D is the average value of the oscillation, and for a rider on a wheel that is the height of the wheel's center, because the rider spends equal time above and below it. Here D=38, so the rider averages \boxed{38\text{ ft}} above the ground.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=16, so the quantity rises 16 above the average value and falls 16 below it:

\text{maximum}=38+16=54\text{ ft}\qquad\text{minimum}=38-16=22\text{ ft}

The rider reaches a maximum of 54\text{ ft} at 6 minutes after the ride starts and a minimum of 22\text{ ft} at 12 minutes after the ride starts, so the range of heights is \boxed{[22\text{ ft},\ 54\text{ ft}]}. That minimum is also the height of the boarding platform.

Part (c). Here B=\frac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\pi/6}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} minutes, and so the wheel makes one full revolution every 12 minutes.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of t that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(t-3)=0 \implies t-3=0 \implies t=3

The phase shift is \boxed{3} minutes, and so the ride is shifted 3 minutes: the rider is at the height of the center and rising at 3 minutes after the ride starts, reaches the top at 6 minutes after the ride starts, and is lowest at 12 minutes after the ride starts.

Part (e). Substitute t=5 (at 5 minutes after the ride starts):

H(5)=16\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(5-3)\right]+38=16\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{3}\right)+38

=16\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)+38=\frac{16\sqrt{3}}{2}+38

So the model gives approximately \boxed{51.9\text{ ft}} at 5 minutes after the ride starts.

data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline of a sinusoid f(x)=A\sin[B(x-h)]+D is y=D, and the midline is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=51, so the average temperature is \boxed{51^\circ\text{F}}.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=20, so the quantity rises 20 above the average value and falls 20 below it:

\text{maximum}=51+20=71^\circ\text{F}\qquad\text{minimum}=51-20=31^\circ\text{F}

The warmest month on average is August and the coolest is February, so the range of monthly average temperatures is \boxed{[31^\circ\text{F},\ 71^\circ\text{F}]}.

Part (c). Here B=\frac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\pi/6}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} months, and so the temperature pattern repeats every 12 months, that is, once each year.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of x that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-5)=0 \implies x-5=0 \implies x=5

The phase shift is \boxed{5} months, and so the sine pattern is shifted 5 months to the right: the temperature is at its average and rising in May, not in January. Equivalently, the warmest month is August and the coolest is February.

Part (e). Substitute x=9 (September):

f(9)=20\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(9-5)\right]+51=20\sin\left(\frac{2\pi}{3}\right)+51

=20\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)+51=\frac{20\sqrt{3}}{2}+51

Part (b). The amplitude is A=20, so the quantity rises 20 above the average value and falls 20 below it:

\text{maximum}=55+20=75^\circ\text{F}\qquad\text{minimum}=55-20=35^\circ\text{F}

The warmest month on average is August and the coolest is February, so the range of monthly average temperatures is \boxed{[35^\circ\text{F},\ 75^\circ\text{F}]}.

Part (c). Here B=\frac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\pi/6}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} months, and so the temperature pattern repeats every 12 months, that is, once each year.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of x that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-5)=0 \implies x-5=0 \implies x=5

The phase shift is \boxed{5} months, and so the sine pattern is shifted 5 months to the right: the temperature is at its average and rising in May, not in January. Equivalently, the warmest month is August and the coolest is February.

Part (e). Substitute x=7 (July):

f(7)=20\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(7-5)\right]+55=20\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{3}\right)+55

\text{maximum}=10+4=14\text{ ft}\qquad\text{minimum}=10-4=6\text{ ft}

Part (c). Here B=\frac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\pi/6}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-2)=0 \implies x-2=0 \implies x=2

data.part_b: What are the highest and lowest water levels of the reservoir?
data.part_c: What is the period of this function, and what does it mean in this context?
data.part_d: What is the phase shift of this function, and what does it mean in this context?
data.part_e: Use the model to estimate the water level in December. Round to the nearest tenth of a foot.
data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline y=D is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=18, so the reservoir averages \boxed{18\text{ ft}}.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=8, so the quantity rises 8 above the average value and falls 8 below it:

\text{maximum}=18+8=26\text{ ft}\qquad\text{minimum}=18-8=10\text{ ft}

The reservoir is highest in July at 26\text{ ft} and lowest in January at 10\text{ ft}, so the range of levels is \boxed{[10\text{ ft},\ 26\text{ ft}]}.

Part (c). Here B=\frac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\pi/6}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} months, and so the level follows a yearly cycle and repeats every 12 months.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of x that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-4)=0 \implies x-4=0 \implies x=4

The phase shift is \boxed{4} months, and so the pattern is shifted 4 months to the right: the level is at its average and rising in April, peaks in July, and is lowest in January.

Part (e). Substitute x=12 (December):

L(12)=8\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(12-4)\right]+18=8\sin\left(\frac{4\pi}{3}\right)+18

=8\left(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)+18=-\frac{8\sqrt{3}}{2}+18

So the model gives approximately \boxed{11.1\text{ ft}} in December.

data.scenario_text: The function d(x)=6\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(x-4)\right]+14 models the depth of the water, in feet, at a harbor, where x=0 represents midnight and x is the number of hours after midnight.
data.part_a: What is the average depth of the water at this harbor?
data.part_b: What are the greatest and least depths of the water at this harbor?
data.part_c: What is the period of this function? How many times does high tide occur in a day?
data.part_d: What is the phase shift of this function, and what does it mean in this context?
data.part_e: Use the model to estimate the depth of the water at 5:00 a.m.. Round to the nearest tenth of a foot.
data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline of a sinusoid d(x)=A\sin[B(x-h)]+D is y=D, and the midline is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=14, so the water averages \boxed{14\text{ ft}} deep.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=6, so the quantity rises 6 above the average value and falls 6 below it:

\text{maximum}=14+6=20\text{ ft}\qquad\text{minimum}=14-6=8\text{ ft}

High tide is at 7:00 a.m., when the depth is 20\text{ ft}, and low tide is at 1:00 p.m., when the depth is 8\text{ ft}, so the range of depths is \boxed{[8\text{ ft},\ 20\text{ ft}]}.

Part (c). Here B=\frac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\pi/6}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} hours, and so the water returns to the same depth every 12 hours. High tide therefore occurs twice in a 24-hour day, and low tide twice as well.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of x that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-4)=0 \implies x-4=0 \implies x=4

The phase shift is \boxed{4} hours, and so the pattern is shifted 4 hours to the right: at 4:00 a.m. the water is at its average depth and rising. High tide is at 7:00 a.m. and again at 7:00 p.m.; low tide is at 1:00 p.m. and again at 1:00 a.m..

Part (e). Substitute x=5 (5:00 a.m.):

d(5)=6\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(5-4)\right]+14=6\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{6}\right)+14

data.part_e: Use the model to estimate the average temperature in May. Round to the nearest tenth of a degree.
data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline of a sinusoid y=A\sin[B(x-h)]+D is y=D, and the midline is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=51, so the average temperature is \boxed{51^\circ\text{F}}.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=@A@, so the quantity rises @A@ above the average value and falls @A@ below it:

\text{maximum}=51+14=65^\circ\text{F}\qquad \text{minimum}=51-14=37^\circ\text{F}

the warmest month on average is June and the coolest is December, so the range of monthly average temperatures is \boxed{[37^\circ\text{F},\ 65^\circ\text{F}]}.

Part (c). Here B= rac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\frac{\pi}{6}}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} @index_unit@, and so the temperature pattern repeats every 12 months, that is, once each year.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of @var@ that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-3)=0 \implies x-3=0 \implies x=3

The phase shift is \boxed{3} months, and so the sine pattern is shifted 3 months to the right: the temperature is at its average and rising in March, not in January. Equivalently, the warmest month is June and the coolest is December.

Part (e). Substitute x=5 (May):

f(5)=14\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(5-3)\right]+51=14\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)+51=7 \, \sqrt{3} + 51 \approx 63.1^\circ\text{F}

So the model predicts an average temperature of about \boxed{63.1^\circ\text{F}} in May.

data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline of a sinusoid y=A\sin[B(x-h)]+D is y=D, and the midline is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=54, so the average temperature is \boxed{54^\circ\text{F}}.

\text{maximum}=54+18=72^\circ\text{F}\qquad \text{minimum}=54-18=36^\circ\text{F}

Part (c). Here B= rac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\frac{\pi}{6}}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} @index_unit@, and so the temperature pattern repeats every 12 months, that is, once each year.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of @var@ that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-4)=0 \implies x-4=0 \implies x=4

data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline of a sinusoid y=A\sin[B(x-h)]+D is y=D, and the midline is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=59, so the average temperature is \boxed{59^\circ\text{F}}.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=@A@, so the quantity rises @A@ above the average value and falls @A@ below it:

\text{maximum}=59+16=75^\circ\text{F}\qquad \text{minimum}=59-16=43^\circ\text{F}

the warmest month on average is July and the coolest is January, so the range of monthly average temperatures is \boxed{[43^\circ\text{F},\ 75^\circ\text{F}]}.

Part (c). Here B= rac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\frac{\pi}{6}}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} @index_unit@, and so the temperature pattern repeats every 12 months, that is, once each year.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of @var@ that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

data.scenario_text: The function <me>d(x)=4\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(x-2)\right]+13</me> models the depth of the water, in feet, at a harbor, where <m>x</m> is the number of hours after midnight and <m>x=0</m> represents midnight.
data.part_a: What is the average depth of the water at this harbor?
data.part_b: What are the greatest and least depths of the water at this harbor?
data.part_c: What is the period of this function? How many times a day does high tide occur?
data.part_d: What is the phase shift of this function, and what does it mean in this context?
data.part_e: Use the model to estimate the depth of the water at 3:00 a.m.. Round to the nearest tenth of a foot.
data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline of a sinusoid y=A\sin[B(x-h)]+D is y=D, and the midline is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=13, so the water averages \boxed{13\text{ ft}} deep.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=@A@, so the quantity rises @A@ above the average value and falls @A@ below it:

\text{maximum}=13+4=17\text{ ft}\qquad \text{minimum}=13-4=9\text{ ft}

high tide is at 5:00 a.m., when the depth is 17\text{ ft}, and low tide is at 11:00 a.m., when the depth is 9\text{ ft}, so the range of depths is \boxed{[9\text{ ft},\ 17\text{ ft}]}.

Part (c). Here B= rac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\frac{\pi}{6}}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} @index_unit@, and so the water returns to the same depth every 12 hours. High tide therefore occurs twice in a 24-hour day, and low tide twice as well.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of @var@ that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-2)=0 \implies x-2=0 \implies x=2

The phase shift is \boxed{2} hours, and so the pattern is shifted 2 hours to the right: at 2:00 a.m. the water is at its average depth and rising. High tide is at 5:00 a.m. and again at 5:00 p.m.; low tide is at 11:00 a.m. and again at 11:00 p.m..

Part (e). Substitute x=3 (3:00 a.m.):

d(3)=4\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(3-2)\right]+13=4\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)+13=17\text{ ft}

So the model predicts a depth of about \boxed{17.0\text{ ft}} at 3:00 a.m..

data.part_c: What is the period of this function? How many times a day does high tide occur?
data.part_d: What is the phase shift of this function, and what does it mean in this context?
data.part_e: Use the model to estimate the depth of the water at 6:00 a.m.. Round to the nearest tenth of a foot.
data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline of a sinusoid y=A\sin[B(x-h)]+D is y=D, and the midline is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=10, so the water averages \boxed{10\text{ ft}} deep.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=@A@, so the quantity rises @A@ above the average value and falls @A@ below it:

\text{maximum}=10+4=14\text{ ft}\qquad \text{minimum}=10-4=6\text{ ft}

high tide is at 7:00 a.m., when the depth is 14\text{ ft}, and low tide is at 1:00 p.m., when the depth is 6\text{ ft}, so the range of depths is \boxed{[6\text{ ft},\ 14\text{ ft}]}.

Part (c). Here B= rac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\frac{\pi}{6}}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} @index_unit@, and so the water returns to the same depth every 12 hours. High tide therefore occurs twice in a 24-hour day, and low tide twice as well.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of @var@ that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-4)=0 \implies x-4=0 \implies x=4

The phase shift is \boxed{4} hours, and so the pattern is shifted 4 hours to the right: at 4:00 a.m. the water is at its average depth and rising. High tide is at 7:00 a.m. and again at 7:00 p.m.; low tide is at 1:00 p.m. and again at 1:00 a.m..

Part (e). Substitute x=6 (6:00 a.m.):

d(6)=4\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(6-4)\right]+10=4\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)+10=2 \, \sqrt{3} + 10 \approx 13.5\text{ ft}

So the model predicts a depth of about \boxed{13.5\text{ ft}} at 6:00 a.m..

Part (a). The midline of a sinusoid y=A\sin[B(x-h)]+D is y=D, and the midline is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=9, so the water averages \boxed{9\text{ ft}} deep.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=@A@, so the quantity rises @A@ above the average value and falls @A@ below it:

\text{maximum}=9+6=15\text{ ft}\qquad \text{minimum}=9-6=3\text{ ft}

high tide is at 8:00 a.m., when the depth is 15\text{ ft}, and low tide is at 2:00 p.m., when the depth is 3\text{ ft}, so the range of depths is \boxed{[3\text{ ft},\ 15\text{ ft}]}.

Part (c). Here B= rac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

The period is \boxed{12} @index_unit@, and so the water returns to the same depth every 12 hours. High tide therefore occurs twice in a 24-hour day, and low tide twice as well.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of @var@ that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-5)=0 \implies x-5=0 \implies x=5

data.part_b: What are the greatest and least depths of the water at this harbor?
data.part_c: What is the period of this function? How many times a day does high tide occur?
data.part_d: What is the phase shift of this function, and what does it mean in this context?
data.part_e: Use the model to estimate the depth of the water at 10:00 a.m.. Round to the nearest tenth of a foot.
data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline of a sinusoid y=A\sin[B(x-h)]+D is y=D, and the midline is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=14, so the water averages \boxed{14\text{ ft}} deep.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=@A@, so the quantity rises @A@ above the average value and falls @A@ below it:

\text{maximum}=14+6=20\text{ ft}\qquad \text{minimum}=14-6=8\text{ ft}

high tide is at 6:00 a.m., when the depth is 20\text{ ft}, and low tide is at noon, when the depth is 8\text{ ft}, so the range of depths is \boxed{[8\text{ ft},\ 20\text{ ft}]}.

Part (c). Here B= rac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\frac{\pi}{6}}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} @index_unit@, and so the water returns to the same depth every 12 hours. High tide therefore occurs twice in a 24-hour day, and low tide twice as well.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of @var@ that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-3)=0 \implies x-3=0 \implies x=3

The phase shift is \boxed{3} hours, and so the pattern is shifted 3 hours to the right: at 3:00 a.m. the water is at its average depth and rising. High tide is at 6:00 a.m. and again at 6:00 p.m.; low tide is at noon and again at midnight.

Part (e). Substitute x=10 (10:00 a.m.):

d(10)=6\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(10-3)\right]+14=6\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)+14=8\text{ ft}

So the model predicts a depth of about \boxed{8.0\text{ ft}} at 10:00 a.m..

data.part_b: What are the greatest and least depths of the water at this harbor?
data.part_c: What is the period of this function? How many times a day does high tide occur?
data.part_d: What is the phase shift of this function, and what does it mean in this context?
data.part_e: Use the model to estimate the depth of the water at 4:00 a.m.. Round to the nearest tenth of a foot.
data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline of a sinusoid y=A\sin[B(x-h)]+D is y=D, and the midline is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=14, so the water averages \boxed{14\text{ ft}} deep.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=@A@, so the quantity rises @A@ above the average value and falls @A@ below it:

\text{maximum}=14+4=18\text{ ft}\qquad \text{minimum}=14-4=10\text{ ft}

high tide is at 6:00 a.m., when the depth is 18\text{ ft}, and low tide is at noon, when the depth is 10\text{ ft}, so the range of depths is \boxed{[10\text{ ft},\ 18\text{ ft}]}.

Part (c). Here B= rac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\frac{\pi}{6}}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} @index_unit@, and so the water returns to the same depth every 12 hours. High tide therefore occurs twice in a 24-hour day, and low tide twice as well.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of @var@ that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-3)=0 \implies x-3=0 \implies x=3

The phase shift is \boxed{3} hours, and so the pattern is shifted 3 hours to the right: at 3:00 a.m. the water is at its average depth and rising. High tide is at 6:00 a.m. and again at 6:00 p.m.; low tide is at noon and again at midnight.

Part (e). Substitute x=4 (4:00 a.m.):

d(4)=4\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(4-3)\right]+14=4\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)+14=18\text{ ft}

So the model predicts a depth of about \boxed{18.0\text{ ft}} at 4:00 a.m..

\text{maximum}=11+6=17\text{ ft}\qquad \text{minimum}=11-6=5\text{ ft}

high tide is at 5:00 a.m., when the depth is 17\text{ ft}, and low tide is at 11:00 a.m., when the depth is 5\text{ ft}, so the range of depths is \boxed{[5\text{ ft},\ 17\text{ ft}]}.

data.part_c: What is the period of this function? How many times a day does high tide occur?
data.part_d: What is the phase shift of this function, and what does it mean in this context?
data.part_e: Use the model to estimate the depth of the water at 9:00 a.m.. Round to the nearest tenth of a foot.
data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline of a sinusoid y=A\sin[B(x-h)]+D is y=D, and the midline is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=15, so the water averages \boxed{15\text{ ft}} deep.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=@A@, so the quantity rises @A@ above the average value and falls @A@ below it:

\text{maximum}=15+4=19\text{ ft}\qquad \text{minimum}=15-4=11\text{ ft}

high tide is at 5:00 a.m., when the depth is 19\text{ ft}, and low tide is at 11:00 a.m., when the depth is 11\text{ ft}, so the range of depths is \boxed{[11\text{ ft},\ 19\text{ ft}]}.

Part (c). Here B= rac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\frac{\pi}{6}}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} @index_unit@, and so the water returns to the same depth every 12 hours. High tide therefore occurs twice in a 24-hour day, and low tide twice as well.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of @var@ that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-2)=0 \implies x-2=0 \implies x=2

The phase shift is \boxed{2} hours, and so the pattern is shifted 2 hours to the right: at 2:00 a.m. the water is at its average depth and rising. High tide is at 5:00 a.m. and again at 5:00 p.m.; low tide is at 11:00 a.m. and again at 11:00 p.m..

Part (e). Substitute x=9 (9:00 a.m.):

d(9)=4\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(9-2)\right]+15=4\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)+15=11\text{ ft}

So the model predicts a depth of about \boxed{11.0\text{ ft}} at 9:00 a.m..

data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline of a sinusoid y=A\sin[B(x-h)]+D is y=D, and the midline is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=12, so the water averages \boxed{12\text{ ft}} deep.

\text{maximum}=12+6=18\text{ ft}\qquad \text{minimum}=12-6=6\text{ ft}

high tide is at 5:00 a.m., when the depth is 18\text{ ft}, and low tide is at 11:00 a.m., when the depth is 6\text{ ft}, so the range of depths is \boxed{[6\text{ ft},\ 18\text{ ft}]}.

Part (c). Here B= rac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

data.part_b: What are the greatest and least depths of the water at this harbor?
data.part_c: What is the period of this function? How many times a day does high tide occur?
data.part_d: What is the phase shift of this function, and what does it mean in this context?
data.part_e: Use the model to estimate the depth of the water at 10:00 a.m.. Round to the nearest tenth of a foot.
data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline of a sinusoid y=A\sin[B(x-h)]+D is y=D, and the midline is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=14, so the water averages \boxed{14\text{ ft}} deep.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=@A@, so the quantity rises @A@ above the average value and falls @A@ below it:

\text{maximum}=14+4=18\text{ ft}\qquad \text{minimum}=14-4=10\text{ ft}

high tide is at 6:00 a.m., when the depth is 18\text{ ft}, and low tide is at noon, when the depth is 10\text{ ft}, so the range of depths is \boxed{[10\text{ ft},\ 18\text{ ft}]}.

Part (c). Here B= rac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\frac{\pi}{6}}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} @index_unit@, and so the water returns to the same depth every 12 hours. High tide therefore occurs twice in a 24-hour day, and low tide twice as well.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of @var@ that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-3)=0 \implies x-3=0 \implies x=3

The phase shift is \boxed{3} hours, and so the pattern is shifted 3 hours to the right: at 3:00 a.m. the water is at its average depth and rising. High tide is at 6:00 a.m. and again at 6:00 p.m.; low tide is at noon and again at midnight.

Part (e). Substitute x=10 (10:00 a.m.):

d(10)=4\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(10-3)\right]+14=4\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)+14=10\text{ ft}

So the model predicts a depth of about \boxed{10.0\text{ ft}} at 10:00 a.m..

data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline of a sinusoid y=A\sin[B(x-h)]+D is y=D, and the midline is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=9, so the water averages \boxed{9\text{ ft}} deep.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=@A@, so the quantity rises @A@ above the average value and falls @A@ below it:

\text{maximum}=9+6=15\text{ ft}\qquad \text{minimum}=9-6=3\text{ ft}

high tide is at 5:00 a.m., when the depth is 15\text{ ft}, and low tide is at 11:00 a.m., when the depth is 3\text{ ft}, so the range of depths is \boxed{[3\text{ ft},\ 15\text{ ft}]}.

Part (c). Here B= rac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\frac{\pi}{6}}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} @index_unit@, and so the water returns to the same depth every 12 hours. High tide therefore occurs twice in a 24-hour day, and low tide twice as well.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of @var@ that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-2)=0 \implies x-2=0 \implies x=2

\text{maximum}=13+6=19\text{ ft}\qquad \text{minimum}=13-6=7\text{ ft}

high tide is at 6:00 a.m., when the depth is 19\text{ ft}, and low tide is at noon, when the depth is 7\text{ ft}, so the range of depths is \boxed{[7\text{ ft},\ 19\text{ ft}]}.

Part (c). Here B= rac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-3)=0 \implies x-3=0 \implies x=3

data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline of a sinusoid y=A\sin[B(x-h)]+D is y=D, and the midline is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=15, so the water averages \boxed{15\text{ ft}} deep.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=@A@, so the quantity rises @A@ above the average value and falls @A@ below it:

\text{maximum}=15+6=21\text{ ft}\qquad \text{minimum}=15-6=9\text{ ft}

high tide is at 8:00 a.m., when the depth is 21\text{ ft}, and low tide is at 2:00 p.m., when the depth is 9\text{ ft}, so the range of depths is \boxed{[9\text{ ft},\ 21\text{ ft}]}.

Part (c). Here B= rac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\frac{\pi}{6}}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} @index_unit@, and so the water returns to the same depth every 12 hours. High tide therefore occurs twice in a 24-hour day, and low tide twice as well.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of @var@ that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-5)=0 \implies x-5=0 \implies x=5

Part (a). The midline of a sinusoid y=A\sin[B(x-h)]+D is y=D, and the midline is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=13, so the water averages \boxed{13\text{ ft}} deep.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=@A@, so the quantity rises @A@ above the average value and falls @A@ below it:

\text{maximum}=13+4=17\text{ ft}\qquad \text{minimum}=13-4=9\text{ ft}

high tide is at 6:00 a.m., when the depth is 17\text{ ft}, and low tide is at noon, when the depth is 9\text{ ft}, so the range of depths is \boxed{[9\text{ ft},\ 17\text{ ft}]}.

Part (c). Here B= rac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\frac{\pi}{6}}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline of a sinusoid y=A\sin[B(x-h)]+D is y=D, and the midline is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=9, so the water averages \boxed{9\text{ ft}} deep.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=@A@, so the quantity rises @A@ above the average value and falls @A@ below it:

\text{maximum}=9+4=13\text{ ft}\qquad \text{minimum}=9-4=5\text{ ft}

high tide is at 8:00 a.m., when the depth is 13\text{ ft}, and low tide is at 2:00 p.m., when the depth is 5\text{ ft}, so the range of depths is \boxed{[5\text{ ft},\ 13\text{ ft}]}.

Part (c). Here B= rac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

data.part_c: What is the period of this function? How many times a day does high tide occur?
data.part_d: What is the phase shift of this function, and what does it mean in this context?
data.part_e: Use the model to estimate the depth of the water at 6:00 a.m.. Round to the nearest tenth of a foot.
data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline of a sinusoid y=A\sin[B(x-h)]+D is y=D, and the midline is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=15, so the water averages \boxed{15\text{ ft}} deep.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=@A@, so the quantity rises @A@ above the average value and falls @A@ below it:

\text{maximum}=15+4=19\text{ ft}\qquad \text{minimum}=15-4=11\text{ ft}

high tide is at 5:00 a.m., when the depth is 19\text{ ft}, and low tide is at 11:00 a.m., when the depth is 11\text{ ft}, so the range of depths is \boxed{[11\text{ ft},\ 19\text{ ft}]}.

Part (c). Here B= rac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\frac{\pi}{6}}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} @index_unit@, and so the water returns to the same depth every 12 hours. High tide therefore occurs twice in a 24-hour day, and low tide twice as well.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of @var@ that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-2)=0 \implies x-2=0 \implies x=2

The phase shift is \boxed{2} hours, and so the pattern is shifted 2 hours to the right: at 2:00 a.m. the water is at its average depth and rising. High tide is at 5:00 a.m. and again at 5:00 p.m.; low tide is at 11:00 a.m. and again at 11:00 p.m..

Part (e). Substitute x=6 (6:00 a.m.):

d(6)=4\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(6-2)\right]+15=4\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)+15=2 \, \sqrt{3} + 15 \approx 18.5\text{ ft}

So the model predicts a depth of about \boxed{18.5\text{ ft}} at 6:00 a.m..

Part (a). The midline of a sinusoid y=A\sin[B(x-h)]+D is y=D, and the midline is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=9, so the water averages \boxed{9\text{ ft}} deep.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=@A@, so the quantity rises @A@ above the average value and falls @A@ below it:

\text{maximum}=9+6=15\text{ ft}\qquad \text{minimum}=9-6=3\text{ ft}

high tide is at 8:00 a.m., when the depth is 15\text{ ft}, and low tide is at 2:00 p.m., when the depth is 3\text{ ft}, so the range of depths is \boxed{[3\text{ ft},\ 15\text{ ft}]}.

Part (c). Here B= rac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\frac{\pi}{6}}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} @index_unit@, and so the water returns to the same depth every 12 hours. High tide therefore occurs twice in a 24-hour day, and low tide twice as well.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of @var@ that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-5)=0 \implies x-5=0 \implies x=5

The phase shift is \boxed{5} hours, and so the pattern is shifted 5 hours to the right: at 5:00 a.m. the water is at its average depth and rising. High tide is at 8:00 a.m. and again at 8:00 p.m.; low tide is at 2:00 p.m. and again at 2:00 a.m..

high tide is at 6:00 a.m., when the depth is 15\text{ ft}, and low tide is at noon, when the depth is 3\text{ ft}, so the range of depths is \boxed{[3\text{ ft},\ 15\text{ ft}]}.

Part (c). Here B= rac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\frac{\pi}{6}}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

data.part_e: Use the model to estimate the number of hours of daylight in November. Round to the nearest tenth of an hour.
data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline y=D is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=12, so the city averages \boxed{12\text{ hr}} of daylight.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=@A@, so the quantity rises @A@ above the average value and falls @A@ below it:

\text{maximum}=12+2=14\text{ hr}\qquad \text{minimum}=12-2=10\text{ hr}

the longest day is in December, with 14\text{ hr} of daylight, and the shortest is in June, with 10\text{ hr}, so the range is \boxed{[10\text{ hr},\ 14\text{ hr}]}.

Part (c). Here B= rac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\frac{\pi}{6}}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} @index_unit@, and so the daylight pattern repeats every 12 months, that is, once each year.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of @var@ that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-9)=0 \implies x-9=0 \implies x=9

The phase shift is \boxed{9} months, and so the pattern is shifted 9 months to the right: daylight is at its average and increasing in September, which is an equinox. The longest day falls in December and the shortest in June, as expected in the Southern Hemisphere.

Part (e). Substitute x=11 (November):

L(11)=2\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(11-9)\right]+12=2\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)+12=\sqrt{3} + 12 \approx 13.7\text{ hr}

So the model predicts about \boxed{13.7\text{ hr}} of daylight in November.

data.part_e: Use the model to estimate the number of hours of daylight in October. Round to the nearest tenth of an hour.
data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline y=D is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=12, so the city averages \boxed{12\text{ hr}} of daylight.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=@A@, so the quantity rises @A@ above the average value and falls @A@ below it:

\text{maximum}=12+2=14\text{ hr}\qquad \text{minimum}=12-2=10\text{ hr}

the longest day is in December, with 14\text{ hr} of daylight, and the shortest is in June, with 10\text{ hr}, so the range is \boxed{[10\text{ hr},\ 14\text{ hr}]}.

Part (c). Here B= rac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\frac{\pi}{6}}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} @index_unit@, and so the daylight pattern repeats every 12 months, that is, once each year.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of @var@ that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-9)=0 \implies x-9=0 \implies x=9

The phase shift is \boxed{9} months, and so the pattern is shifted 9 months to the right: daylight is at its average and increasing in September, which is an equinox. The longest day falls in December and the shortest in June, as expected in the Southern Hemisphere.

Part (e). Substitute x=10 (October):

L(10)=2\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(10-9)\right]+12=2\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)+12=14\text{ hr}

So the model predicts about \boxed{14.0\text{ hr}} of daylight in October.

data.part_b: What is the range of the number of hours of daylight in this city?
data.part_c: What is the period of this function, and what does it mean in this context?
data.part_d: What is the phase shift of this function, and what does it mean in this context?
data.part_e: Use the model to estimate the number of hours of daylight in July. Round to the nearest tenth of an hour.
data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline y=D is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=12, so the city averages \boxed{12\text{ hr}} of daylight.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=@A@, so the quantity rises @A@ above the average value and falls @A@ below it:

\text{maximum}=12+2=14\text{ hr}\qquad \text{minimum}=12-2=10\text{ hr}

the longest day is in June, with 14\text{ hr} of daylight, and the shortest is in December, with 10\text{ hr}, so the range is \boxed{[10\text{ hr},\ 14\text{ hr}]}.

Part (c). Here B= rac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\frac{\pi}{6}}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} @index_unit@, and so the daylight pattern repeats every 12 months, that is, once each year.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of @var@ that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-3)=0 \implies x-3=0 \implies x=3

The phase shift is \boxed{3} months, and so the pattern is shifted 3 months to the right: daylight is at its average and increasing in March, which is an equinox. The longest day falls in June and the shortest in December, as expected in the Northern Hemisphere.

Part (e). Substitute x=7 (July):

L(7)=2\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(7-3)\right]+12=2\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)+12=\sqrt{3} + 12 \approx 13.7\text{ hr}

So the model predicts about \boxed{13.7\text{ hr}} of daylight in July.

data.part_e: Use the model to estimate the number of hours of daylight in April. Round to the nearest tenth of an hour.
data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline y=D is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=12, so the city averages \boxed{12\text{ hr}} of daylight.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=@A@, so the quantity rises @A@ above the average value and falls @A@ below it:

\text{maximum}=12+4=16\text{ hr}\qquad \text{minimum}=12-4=8\text{ hr}

the longest day is in June, with 16\text{ hr} of daylight, and the shortest is in December, with 8\text{ hr}, so the range is \boxed{[8\text{ hr},\ 16\text{ hr}]}.

Part (c). Here B= rac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\frac{\pi}{6}}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} @index_unit@, and so the daylight pattern repeats every 12 months, that is, once each year.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of @var@ that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-3)=0 \implies x-3=0 \implies x=3

The phase shift is \boxed{3} months, and so the pattern is shifted 3 months to the right: daylight is at its average and increasing in March, which is an equinox. The longest day falls in June and the shortest in December, as expected in the Northern Hemisphere.

Part (e). Substitute x=4 (April):

L(4)=4\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(4-3)\right]+12=4\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)+12=16\text{ hr}

So the model predicts about \boxed{16.0\text{ hr}} of daylight in April.

data.part_b: What is the range of the number of hours of daylight in this city?
data.part_c: What is the period of this function, and what does it mean in this context?
data.part_d: What is the phase shift of this function, and what does it mean in this context?
data.part_e: Use the model to estimate the number of hours of daylight in April. Round to the nearest tenth of an hour.
data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline y=D is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=12, so the city averages \boxed{12\text{ hr}} of daylight.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=@A@, so the quantity rises @A@ above the average value and falls @A@ below it:

\text{maximum}=12+4=16\text{ hr}\qquad \text{minimum}=12-4=8\text{ hr}

the longest day is in June, with 16\text{ hr} of daylight, and the shortest is in December, with 8\text{ hr}, so the range is \boxed{[8\text{ hr},\ 16\text{ hr}]}.

Part (c). Here B= rac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\frac{\pi}{6}}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} @index_unit@, and so the daylight pattern repeats every 12 months, that is, once each year.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of @var@ that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-3)=0 \implies x-3=0 \implies x=3

The phase shift is \boxed{3} months, and so the pattern is shifted 3 months to the right: daylight is at its average and increasing in March, which is an equinox. The longest day falls in June and the shortest in December, as expected in the Northern Hemisphere.

Part (e). Substitute x=4 (April):

L(4)=4\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(4-3)\right]+12=4\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)+12=16\text{ hr}

So the model predicts about \boxed{16.0\text{ hr}} of daylight in April.

data.part_b: What is the range of the number of hours of daylight in this city?
data.part_c: What is the period of this function, and what does it mean in this context?
data.part_d: What is the phase shift of this function, and what does it mean in this context?
data.part_e: Use the model to estimate the number of hours of daylight in November. Round to the nearest tenth of an hour.
data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline y=D is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=12, so the city averages \boxed{12\text{ hr}} of daylight.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=@A@, so the quantity rises @A@ above the average value and falls @A@ below it:

\text{maximum}=12+4=16\text{ hr}\qquad \text{minimum}=12-4=8\text{ hr}

the longest day is in December, with 16\text{ hr} of daylight, and the shortest is in June, with 8\text{ hr}, so the range is \boxed{[8\text{ hr},\ 16\text{ hr}]}.

Part (c). Here B= rac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\frac{\pi}{6}}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} @index_unit@, and so the daylight pattern repeats every 12 months, that is, once each year.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of @var@ that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-9)=0 \implies x-9=0 \implies x=9

The phase shift is \boxed{9} months, and so the pattern is shifted 9 months to the right: daylight is at its average and increasing in September, which is an equinox. The longest day falls in December and the shortest in June, as expected in the Southern Hemisphere.

Part (e). Substitute x=11 (November):

L(11)=4\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(11-9)\right]+12=4\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)+12=2 \, \sqrt{3} + 12 \approx 15.5\text{ hr}

So the model predicts about \boxed{15.5\text{ hr}} of daylight in November.

data.part_b: What is the range of the number of hours of daylight in this city?
data.part_c: What is the period of this function, and what does it mean in this context?
data.part_d: What is the phase shift of this function, and what does it mean in this context?
data.part_e: Use the model to estimate the number of hours of daylight in October. Round to the nearest tenth of an hour.
data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline y=D is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=12, so the city averages \boxed{12\text{ hr}} of daylight.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=@A@, so the quantity rises @A@ above the average value and falls @A@ below it:

\text{maximum}=12+4=16\text{ hr}\qquad \text{minimum}=12-4=8\text{ hr}

the longest day is in December, with 16\text{ hr} of daylight, and the shortest is in June, with 8\text{ hr}, so the range is \boxed{[8\text{ hr},\ 16\text{ hr}]}.

Part (c). Here B= rac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\frac{\pi}{6}}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} @index_unit@, and so the daylight pattern repeats every 12 months, that is, once each year.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of @var@ that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-9)=0 \implies x-9=0 \implies x=9

The phase shift is \boxed{9} months, and so the pattern is shifted 9 months to the right: daylight is at its average and increasing in September, which is an equinox. The longest day falls in December and the shortest in June, as expected in the Southern Hemisphere.

Part (e). Substitute x=10 (October):

L(10)=4\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(10-9)\right]+12=4\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)+12=16\text{ hr}

So the model predicts about \boxed{16.0\text{ hr}} of daylight in October.

data.part_e: Use the model to estimate the number of hours of daylight in August. Round to the nearest tenth of an hour.
data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline y=D is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=12, so the city averages \boxed{12\text{ hr}} of daylight.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=@A@, so the quantity rises @A@ above the average value and falls @A@ below it:

\text{maximum}=12+2=14\text{ hr}\qquad \text{minimum}=12-2=10\text{ hr}

the longest day is in June, with 14\text{ hr} of daylight, and the shortest is in December, with 10\text{ hr}, so the range is \boxed{[10\text{ hr},\ 14\text{ hr}]}.

Part (c). Here B= rac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\frac{\pi}{6}}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} @index_unit@, and so the daylight pattern repeats every 12 months, that is, once each year.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of @var@ that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-3)=0 \implies x-3=0 \implies x=3

The phase shift is \boxed{3} months, and so the pattern is shifted 3 months to the right: daylight is at its average and increasing in March, which is an equinox. The longest day falls in June and the shortest in December, as expected in the Northern Hemisphere.

Part (e). Substitute x=8 (August):

L(8)=2\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(8-3)\right]+12=2\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)+12=14\text{ hr}

So the model predicts about \boxed{14.0\text{ hr}} of daylight in August.

data.part_b: What is the range of the number of hours of daylight in this city?
data.part_c: What is the period of this function, and what does it mean in this context?
data.part_d: What is the phase shift of this function, and what does it mean in this context?
data.part_e: Use the model to estimate the number of hours of daylight in April. Round to the nearest tenth of an hour.
data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline y=D is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=12, so the city averages \boxed{12\text{ hr}} of daylight.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=@A@, so the quantity rises @A@ above the average value and falls @A@ below it:

\text{maximum}=12+4=16\text{ hr}\qquad \text{minimum}=12-4=8\text{ hr}

the longest day is in June, with 16\text{ hr} of daylight, and the shortest is in December, with 8\text{ hr}, so the range is \boxed{[8\text{ hr},\ 16\text{ hr}]}.

Part (c). Here B= rac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\frac{\pi}{6}}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} @index_unit@, and so the daylight pattern repeats every 12 months, that is, once each year.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of @var@ that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-3)=0 \implies x-3=0 \implies x=3

The phase shift is \boxed{3} months, and so the pattern is shifted 3 months to the right: daylight is at its average and increasing in March, which is an equinox. The longest day falls in June and the shortest in December, as expected in the Northern Hemisphere.

Part (e). Substitute x=4 (April):

L(4)=4\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(4-3)\right]+12=4\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)+12=16\text{ hr}

So the model predicts about \boxed{16.0\text{ hr}} of daylight in April.

data.part_b: What is the range of the number of hours of daylight in this city?
data.part_c: What is the period of this function, and what does it mean in this context?
data.part_d: What is the phase shift of this function, and what does it mean in this context?
data.part_e: Use the model to estimate the number of hours of daylight in November. Round to the nearest tenth of an hour.
data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline y=D is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=12, so the city averages \boxed{12\text{ hr}} of daylight.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=@A@, so the quantity rises @A@ above the average value and falls @A@ below it:

\text{maximum}=12+4=16\text{ hr}\qquad \text{minimum}=12-4=8\text{ hr}

the longest day is in December, with 16\text{ hr} of daylight, and the shortest is in June, with 8\text{ hr}, so the range is \boxed{[8\text{ hr},\ 16\text{ hr}]}.

Part (c). Here B= rac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\frac{\pi}{6}}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} @index_unit@, and so the daylight pattern repeats every 12 months, that is, once each year.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of @var@ that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-9)=0 \implies x-9=0 \implies x=9

The phase shift is \boxed{9} months, and so the pattern is shifted 9 months to the right: daylight is at its average and increasing in September, which is an equinox. The longest day falls in December and the shortest in June, as expected in the Southern Hemisphere.

Part (e). Substitute x=11 (November):

L(11)=4\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(11-9)\right]+12=4\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)+12=2 \, \sqrt{3} + 12 \approx 15.5\text{ hr}

So the model predicts about \boxed{15.5\text{ hr}} of daylight in November.

data.part_b: What is the range of the number of hours of daylight in this city?
data.part_c: What is the period of this function, and what does it mean in this context?
data.part_d: What is the phase shift of this function, and what does it mean in this context?
data.part_e: Use the model to estimate the number of hours of daylight in May. Round to the nearest tenth of an hour.
data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline y=D is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=12, so the city averages \boxed{12\text{ hr}} of daylight.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=@A@, so the quantity rises @A@ above the average value and falls @A@ below it:

\text{maximum}=12+4=16\text{ hr}\qquad \text{minimum}=12-4=8\text{ hr}

the longest day is in June, with 16\text{ hr} of daylight, and the shortest is in December, with 8\text{ hr}, so the range is \boxed{[8\text{ hr},\ 16\text{ hr}]}.

Part (c). Here B= rac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\frac{\pi}{6}}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} @index_unit@, and so the daylight pattern repeats every 12 months, that is, once each year.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of @var@ that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-3)=0 \implies x-3=0 \implies x=3

The phase shift is \boxed{3} months, and so the pattern is shifted 3 months to the right: daylight is at its average and increasing in March, which is an equinox. The longest day falls in June and the shortest in December, as expected in the Northern Hemisphere.

Part (e). Substitute x=5 (May):

L(5)=4\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(5-3)\right]+12=4\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)+12=2 \, \sqrt{3} + 12 \approx 15.5\text{ hr}

So the model predicts about \boxed{15.5\text{ hr}} of daylight in May.

data.scenario_text: A zipline runs in a straight line from the top of a launch platform to an anchor point on the ground. The zipline is <m>160</m> feet long, and the angle of depression from the top of the platform to the anchor point is <m>21^\circ</m>.
data.part_b: Explain how to place the given <m>21^\circ</m> angle inside the right triangle, then state which trigonometric ratio connects the known sides to the height of the platform.
data.part_c: Find the height of the platform. Do not round until the final answer; then round to two decimal places.
data.solution_steps:
Part (a). A correct sketch shows a right triangle with the 21^\circ angle at the correct vertex, the side opposite it of length 57.34 ft, the side adjacent to it of length 149.37 ft, and the hypotenuse @sh@ ft.

Part (b). The angle of depression is measured downward from a horizontal line through the top of the platform. That line is parallel to the ground, so the angle of depression and the angle of elevation from the anchor point are alternate interior angles and are therefore congruent. The 21^\circ angle sits inside the triangle at the anchor point. The known side is the hypotenuse and the unknown is the height of the platform, so the ratio that connects them is sine: \sin\theta=\dfrac{\text{opposite}}{\text{hypotenuse}}.

Part (c). h=160\sin(21^\circ) \approx 57.34\text{ ft}

So the height of the platform is \boxed{57.34\text{ ft}}.

data.scenario_text: From the top of a lighthouse <m>140</m> feet above sea level, the angle of depression of a boat out at sea is <m>23^\circ</m>.
data.part_b: Explain how to place the given <m>23^\circ</m> angle inside the right triangle, then state which trigonometric ratio connects the known sides to the straight-line distance from the top of the lighthouse to the boat.
data.part_c: Find the straight-line distance from the top of the lighthouse to the boat. Do not round until the final answer; then round to two decimal places.
data.solution_steps:
Part (a). A correct sketch shows a right triangle with the 23^\circ angle at the correct vertex, the side opposite it of length 140 ft, the side adjacent to it of length 329.82 ft, and the hypotenuse @sh@ ft.

data.part_c: Find the horizontal distance from the boat to the foot of the lighthouse. Do not round until the final answer; then round to two decimal places.
data.solution_steps:
Part (a). A correct sketch shows a right triangle with the 32^\circ angle at the correct vertex, the side opposite it of length 90 ft, the side adjacent to it of length 144.03 ft, and the hypotenuse @sh@ ft.

Part (b). The angle of depression is measured downward from a horizontal line through the top of the lighthouse. Because that line is parallel to the surface of the sea, alternate interior angles give a congruent angle of elevation at the boat, so the 32^\circ angle is the one inside the triangle at the boat. The known side is the leg opposite the given angle and the unknown is the horizontal distance from the boat to the foot of the lighthouse, so the ratio that connects them is tangent: \tan\theta=\dfrac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}}.

Part (c). d=\frac{90}{\tan(32^\circ)} \approx 144.03\text{ ft}

So the horizontal distance from the boat to the foot of the lighthouse is \boxed{144.03\text{ ft}}.

data.solution_steps:
Part (a). A correct sketch shows a right triangle with the right angle marked, the given 20^\circ angle placed at the correct vertex, and the one given length written on its correct side: the leg opposite the given angle is 160\text{ ft}. The other two side lengths are not given, so they stay unlabeled. The 20^\circ angle belongs at the boat, not at the top of the lighthouse: the angle of depression stated at the top and the angle of elevation at the boat are alternate interior angles, with the horizontal through the top of the lighthouse parallel to the sea.

Part (b). The angle of depression is measured downward from a horizontal line through the top of the lighthouse. Because that line is parallel to the surface of the sea, alternate interior angles give a congruent angle of elevation at the boat, so the 20^\circ angle is the one inside the triangle at the boat.

Read the triangle from that angle: the horizontal distance from the boat to the foot of the lighthouse is the leg adjacent to the given angle, and the known quantity is the leg opposite the given angle. The one basic ratio that uses exactly those two sides is tangent, \tan\theta=\dfrac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}}, so that is the ratio to use.

Substituting and computing, d=\frac{160}{\tan(20^\circ)}.

So the horizontal distance from the boat to the foot of the lighthouse is \boxed{439.60\text{ ft}}.

data.scenario_text: You stand <m>55</m> feet from the point on the ground directly below a kite. The angle of elevation from your feet to the kite is <m>40^\circ</m>.
data.find_task: Find the height of the kite above the ground. Do not round until the final answer; then round to two decimal places as necessary.
data.solution_steps:
Part (a). A correct sketch shows a right triangle with the right angle marked, the given 40^\circ angle placed at the correct vertex, and the one given length written on its correct side: the leg adjacent to the given angle is 55\text{ ft}. The other two side lengths are not given, so they stay unlabeled. The 40^\circ angle belongs at your feet on the ground, between the horizontal ground and the line of sight to the kite. It is an interior angle of the triangle as stated, so no conversion is needed.

Part (b). The angle of elevation is measured upward from the horizontal ground at your feet, which is already a vertex of the right triangle, so it is an interior angle as given -- no conversion is needed.

Read the triangle from that angle: the height of the kite above the ground is the leg opposite the given angle, and the known quantity is the leg adjacent to the given angle. The one basic ratio that uses exactly those two sides is tangent, \tan\theta=\dfrac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}}, so that is the ratio to use.

Substituting and computing, h=55\tan(40^\circ).

So the height of the kite above the ground is \boxed{46.15\text{ ft}}.

data.scenario_text: A wheelchair ramp is to be built beside the steps to a building. The ramp is <m>32</m> feet long and rises <m>3</m> feet to reach the door.
data.find_task: Find the angle the ramp makes with the ground. Do not round until the final answer; then round to two decimal places as necessary.
data.solution_steps:
Part (a). A correct sketch shows a right triangle with the right angle marked and only the two given lengths written in: the leg opposite \theta is 3\text{ ft} and the hypotenuse is 32\text{ ft}. The third side is not given, so it stays unlabeled, and the angle should not be filled in.

Part (b). Both given quantities are lengths and the unknown is an angle, so the answer comes from an inverse function. In the triangle the given sides are the leg opposite \theta and the hypotenuse; the ratio built from exactly those two sides is sine, \sin\theta=\dfrac{\text{opposite}}{\text{hypotenuse}}, so we solve \sin\theta=\dfrac{\text{opposite}}{\text{hypotenuse}} for \theta using the inverse sine.

Substituting and computing, \theta=\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{3}{32}\right).

This gives \theta \approx 5.38^\circ, so the angle the ramp makes with the ground is \boxed{5.38^\circ}.

outcomes.title: Analyzing Trigonometric Functions
outcomes.description: Analyze the properties of trigonometric functions.
outcomes.template:
For the function below, find the period, the amplitude, and the phase shift. If one of these does not apply to this function, write N/A.

{{{func_tex}}}

Period: ______________________

Amplitude: ______________________

Phase shift: ______________________

 {{{solution_steps}}}

data.solution_steps:
This function has the form y=D+A\,f(Bx+C), with f the sine function. Matching terms gives A=2, B=2, C=-\frac{\pi}{3}, and D=-2. The vertical shift D moves the whole graph up or down, so it changes none of the three quantities asked for; only A, B, and C matter below.

The period of a sine is 2\pi divided by |B|. Here B=2, so the period is \frac{2\pi}{2}=\pi.

The amplitude of a sine is |A|=2, so the amplitude is 2.

With the argument written as Bx+C, the phase shift is the x-value that makes the argument zero. Solving Bx+C=0 gives x=-\dfrac{C}{B}; substituting B=2 and C=-\frac{\pi}{3} gives x=\frac{\pi}{6}, so the graph is shifted \frac{\pi}{6} to the right.
data.answer: Period: pi; Amplitude: 2; Phase shift: pi/6

data.solution_steps:
This function has the form y=D+A\,f(Bx+C), with f the cosine function. Matching terms gives A=-3, B=2, C=\pi, and D=5. The vertical shift D moves the whole graph up or down, so it changes none of the three quantities asked for; only A, B, and C matter below.

The period of a cosine is 2\pi divided by |B|. Here B=2, so the period is \frac{2\pi}{2}=\pi.

The amplitude of a cosine is |A|=3, so the amplitude is 3.

With the argument written as Bx+C, the phase shift is the x-value that makes the argument zero. Solving Bx+C=0 gives x=-\dfrac{C}{B}; substituting B=2 and C=\pi gives x=-\frac{\pi}{2}, so the graph is shifted \frac{\pi}{2} to the left.

This function has the form y=D+A\,f(Bx+C), with f the cosecant function. Matching terms gives A=2, B=2, C=\frac{\pi}{3}, and D=-4. The vertical shift D moves the whole graph up or down, so it changes none of the three quantities asked for; only A, B, and C matter below.

The period of a cosecant is 2\pi divided by |B|. Here B=2, so the period is \frac{2\pi}{2}=\pi.

The cosecant function is unbounded: over one period its values run off to infinity in both directions, so it has no maximum or minimum to measure from a midline. It therefore has no amplitude; write N/A.

With the argument written as Bx+C, the phase shift is the x-value that makes the argument zero. Solving Bx+C=0 gives x=-\dfrac{C}{B}; substituting B=2 and C=\frac{\pi}{3} gives x=-\frac{\pi}{6}, so the graph is shifted \frac{\pi}{6} to the left.
data.answer: Period: pi; Amplitude: N/A; Phase shift: -pi/6

This function has the form y=D+A\,f(Bx+C), with f the cosine function. Matching terms gives A=-2, B=1, C=-\frac{\pi}{3}, and D=0. The vertical shift D moves the whole graph up or down, so it changes none of the three quantities asked for; only A, B, and C matter below.
